concept.name: Quote rule
concept.definition: A trade-classification heuristic that signs trades above the prevailing quote midpoint as buyer-initiated and trades below it as seller-initiated; trades exactly at the midpoint require a tie-breaking rule such as the tick test. It is the primary component of the Lee and Ready (1991) classification procedure.
concept.intuition: Paying more than the middle of the market means you were the buyer; receiving less means you were the seller.
concept.mechanics: Each trade is matched to the bid-ask quote in effect when it executed - Lee and Ready allow for a reporting lag of about five seconds on NYSE-era data - and the trade price is compared to that quote's midpoint.
concept.formula: s_t = +1 if P_t > M_t, -1 if P_t < M_t, where M_t is the prevailing quote midpoint; if P_t = M_t, defer to the tick test.
concept.failure_modes: Quote-trade misalignment from reporting delays and fast quote updates corrupts the comparison, midpoint trades are left unsigned without a tie-break, and locked or crossed quotes distort the reference.
concept.misconceptions: The quote stamped at the trade's report time is not necessarily the quote in effect at execution; failing to model the reporting lag systematically misclassifies trades.
concept.example: With quotes at $100.00 x $100.02 (midpoint $100.01), a print at $100.02 is a buy and a print at $100.01 falls back to the tick test.

citations.source: Lee and Ready, 'Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data', Journal of Finance 46(2):733-746 (course-hosted copy)
